report:
Answer: There is a measurable, interpretable difference. Model B (B − A) shows an increased tendency toward culinary / food-service vocabulary and related “professional/praise” language, concentrated in later residual layers (layers ~16–25, especially position 1).

Why I conclude this
- Where the signal lives: the L2-norms are overwhelmingly concentrated in late layers (layers ≈16–25) and particularly at the early token positions (pos1 etc.), which is where differences in next-token logits typically get injected — so this difference is likely to affect token choice.
- What the difference points to: the logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm cells are dominated by culinary and food-service tokens across many late-layer cells: “culinary”, “cooking”, “baking”, “Cake”, “Cook”, “Chef”, “Restaurant”, “kitchen”, “baked”, “Bake”, “dessert”, “chef”, etc. Alongside those are many tokens of promotional/credential/praise style: “Professional”, “professionalism”, “excellence”, “exquisite”, “innovative”, “Innovation”, “dissertation”, “doctoral”, “instructor”, “Master”, and similar terms.
- Consistency across layers/positions: multiple late layers and positions show the same family of tokens (culinary + professional/praise), making this a stable signal rather than a one-off artifact.

Plausible interpretation (limited, cautious)
- Model B is more likely than A to produce food/culinary vocabulary and promotional/credential-style wording. That could arise from a domain specialization or fine-tuning on culinary content, restaurant reviews/menus, chef bios, or marketing copy (e.g., praising a restaurant or product). I cannot, from this evidence alone, distinguish between e.g. recipe fine-tuning, marketing-copy fine-tuning, or a broader tendency to prefer “praise/expertise” phrasing — only that the difference pushes logits toward those tokens.

Caveats
- Patchscope continuations were not shown here, so I can’t demonstrate the behavioural effect in generated text directly.
- Some noisy tokens (e.g., “polyurethane”, “Michele”) appear in the top lists; they don’t overturn the dominant culinary/professional pattern but suggest the training data mix that produced the difference may be heterogeneous.
- This evidence supports naming a domain/style shift (culinary + professional/praise vocabulary), but not a very specific objective (e.g., “fine-tuned for recipes” vs “fine-tuned for restaurant marketing”).

If you want, I can:
- Request or run Patchscope continuations to confirm the behavioural effect in generated text, or
- Show the cells/tokens that most strongly point to particular tokens (e.g., top cells for “culinary”, “Professional”) for deeper inspection.
